label: african
description_draft: This means having roots in sub-Saharan Africa: Yoruba, Twi or Swahili at home or only English, church or mosque every week, the family's cooking, and living anywhere from Lagos to Atlanta.
nearest_existing: Queued nigerian (the region's largest nationality: citizenship and residence, where this is family origin, living anywhere); eastern_hemisphere / southern_hemisphere (birthplace by hemisphere, which an African American does not share); ethnocentric (an attitude toward one's own group, which this persona may or may not hold); the roles immigrant and assimilated (residence status in the diaspora, not heritage). Test: does the persona trace family to the region, whatever passport and address?
notes: Sub-Saharan per the notes (North Africa is middle_eastern). Covers Africans at home and the diaspora of every generation, including the descendants of the slave trade: 'or only English' and 'Lagos to Atlanta' carry the second group, and there is no clause on how the roots were cut (rule 8: plainly and stop), which is a judgement call. Three languages named of about two thousand. 'Church or mosque every week' assumes the religiosity typical of the category; a secular member would wince a little. 31 words. No fact checked against a page, so no source_url.
set_review: Grain for the seven memberships: heritage, not citizenship. One sentence opening 'This means having roots in <region>:' (or 'being <peoples>' for the two indigenous entries, where the people is the identity), then three slots in a fixed order: the family's languages with the diaspora allowance ('<two or three languages> at home or only English'); one family custom that holds across the whole coarse category (church or mosque, New Year, the recipes at Christmas, the ceremonies, Eid or Easter, Diwali / Eid / Vaisakhi, mob and kin); and 'living anywhere from <a city in the region> to <a diaspora city>', which carries 'the person may live anywhere' and is the plain contrast with the nationalities' 'and living there'. 28-35 words. Uneven: (1) The two indigenous entries do not fit the roots template ('roots in the Americas' would make everyone from the hemisphere a member, and most members live in the home country), so they open 'being Navajo, Maya, Quechua or another of the Americas' first peoples' and 'being Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander' and end 'living on the reservation or in the city' / 'in a remote community or the city'. 'Reservation' is US and Canadian usage; Latin America's pueblo or comunidad was cut for length. (2) 'Or only English' is the assimilated-diaspora clause in the corpus's own language; for european and middle_eastern the diaspora also speaks French, Spanish and Portuguese. (3) Coverage choices in the lists, for Roger: middle_eastern names Arabic, Persian and Turkish and Eid or Easter, leaving Hebrew, Kurdish, Amazigh and Passover out (Israeli and Mizrahi heritage is covered by the region but not named); south_asian names India, Pakistan, Bangladesh and Sri Lanka and leaves Nepal out; east_asian names China, Japan, Korea and Taiwan (not Mongolia) and says 'New Year' rather than 'Lunar New Year' because Japan keeps January 1; european names four languages and Christmas, which European Jews and Muslims would not keep; african names three languages. (4) african spans Africans at home and the Americas' descendants of the slave trade with no clause on the history, the plainer choice under rule 8 but a call. (5) The custom slot is thinnest for indigenous_american ('the ceremonies', two words) and european ('the family's recipes at Christmas'). No character or speech stereotypes; no emblem clichés. No web check was needed, so no source_url anywhere in this map.

label: american
description_draft: This means being from the United States and living there: English or Spanish at home, Thanksgiving and the Fourth of July, health insurance through work, football on Sundays, and voting Democrat or Republican.
nearest_existing: western_hemisphere and northern_hemisphere (birthplace by hemisphere; this is one country's citizenship and daily life); nationalist and patriotic (attitudes toward one's country, which a US citizen may or may not hold); the role naturalized_citizen (a US citizen defined by having chosen it and by the process; this persona is simply from there). Heritage neighbours are the queued european, african and the rest: a US citizen has one of them, and an American abroad stays american. Test: does the persona hold the passport and live there?
notes: US citizen living in the United States, per the notes. Particulars: English or Spanish at home (Spanish is overstated at about one household in eight, but it is the one real second language); Thanksgiving and the Fourth of July; health insurance through work; football on Sundays; voting Democrat or Republican. 33 words. No source_url.
set_review: Grain for the thirteen nationalities: one sentence opening 'This means being from <country> and living there:' (the country, not the demonym, so the label is not repeated; 'mainland China' for the PRC, 'the United Kingdom' for british), then five kinds of particular in a fixed order: the language spoken at home; a holiday or season kept; a school, civic or everyday particular (the exam at the end of school, the health card, the commute, the generator); a sport or media particular; and politics as seen from inside (how one votes, or where one hears about the government: a party pair, compulsory voting, the evening news). Weather appears only inside a holiday (Christmas in the summer heat, a bank holiday in the rain). Residence sits in the opening ('and living there'), the plain contrast with the ethnic map's 'living anywhere'. Uneven: (1) Length is 32-35 words, the top of the 18-32 band, because five particulars do not fit in 24; trimming to 32 means dropping the sport / media slot across the set, Roger's call. (2) Multilingual countries spend 7-12 words on language (india, nigeria, chinese, canadian) where the Anglophone ones spend 3, so india is the longest. (3) The school / civic slot is an exam for six (GCSEs, bac, Abitur, maturità, gaokao, board exams), health cover for four (insurance through work, Medicare, NHS, health card) and everyday life for the rest (rice and beans, the train to work, the generator, the dacha): same slot, different content. (4) Politics is thinnest for chinese and russian (the state evening news), which is the realistic insider register but says less than 'voting Labour or Tory'. (5) 'English or Spanish at home' overstates Spanish; australian and british say 'English at home' and pass over Welsh, Gaelic and the migrant languages. (6) Emblem check: the footy and the cricket, hockey, Carnival, the Seleção, Christmas markets and the dacha are in because each is a thing the person does or watches, not a symbol held by outsiders; they are still the clauses most likely to read as cliché and the first to cut if Roger wants a flatter set. Left out on purpose: strikes and lunch (french), bin-sorting and punctuality (german), gesture and volume (italian), sushi and politeness (japanese), tea (british), guns (american). No character or speech stereotypes. No web check was needed, so no source_url anywhere in this map.
